source: Relationship between Thinking Dispositions, Working Memory, and Critical Thinking Ability in Adolescents (longitudinal, China)
finding: Disposition and ability correlate only modestly. Working memory correlates with critical thinking about as much as the disposition scale does.
numbers: N=509 adolescents (601 at T1, 15.3% lost), mean age 14.09. T1 dispositions-CT r=.29; working memory-CT r=.35; working memory-dispositions r=.10. Cornell Level X alpha .71/.68.
limits: Single measure per construct, no CFA, modest reliabilities (.68-.73), self-report disposition scale.
agent_relevance: Disposition scales explain under 10% of skill variance. A disposition cannot stand in for ability; build checks on outputs, not on declared attitude.

source: Relationship between Thinking Dispositions, Working Memory, and Critical Thinking Ability in Adolescents (longitudinal, China) cross-lagged paths
finding: Over 12 months, working memory predicted later critical thinking more strongly than dispositions did. Critical thinking weakly predicted later dispositions.
numbers: T1 WM->T2 CT beta=.28; T1 dispositions->T2 CT beta=.15; Wald difference chi2(1)=7.27, p=.007. T1 CT->T2 dispositions beta=.10, p=.016. Fit CFI .99, RMSEA .012. Partial r at T2 given T1: WM .12, dispositions .10.
quote: working memory at Time 1 showed a larger predictive effect on critical thinking ability at Time 2
limits: Two waves only; no mediation test; WM was very stable so the reverse path had little variance.
agent_relevance: Capacity (working memory, here context budget) limits skill more than attitude does. Habit is partly an outcome of competence, not only a cause.

source: Orhan and Ceviker Ay (2022) How to teach critical thinking: an experimental study with three different approaches (Learning Environments Research)
finding: Explicit teaching of critical thinking as its own subject raised skills far more than control. All three approaches raised skills; the control did not move.
numbers: N=114 ninth-graders, 4 classes, 10 weeks. General arm (n=29) skills 34.96->47.41, d=3.04; immersion d=3.22; mixed d=3.52; control z=-0.48 p=.63. Posttest Kruskal-Wallis chi2=79.5, eta2=.69.
limits: Quasi-experiment, one school, one instructor, test tied to taught sub-skills (teaching to the test). Text and table degrees of freedom disagree.
agent_relevance: Huge gains on a test matched to the taught content say little about transfer. Count only gains on unfitted items (G3).

source: Orhan and Ceviker Ay (2022), dispositions outcome
finding: Dispositions moved less than skills, and the size depended on the teaching approach. General approach gave the biggest disposition gain.
numbers: UF/EMI CTDI posttest means: general 4.28, mixed 4.00, immersion 3.94, control 3.60. d: general 1.12, immersion 0.74, mixed 0.44. Group ANOVA F=18.1, eta2=.26. Control no change (p=.985).
limits: Self-report instrument; all groups taught by one researcher who knew the hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Dispositions are trainable but self-reported gains are the weakest kind of evidence; verify through behaviour.

source: Building critical thinking in pre-service teachers: Dispositions, skills, and standards (2025)
finding: A 10-week course lifted skills about twice as much as dispositions. Openness rose; reflective skepticism did not.
numbers: n=16 ELT pre-service teachers, no control. Skills d=0.99 (25.31->29.87). Overall disposition d=0.55 (42.00->43.81, p=.04). Critical openness d=0.60 (p=.02). Reflective skepticism 15.43->16.12, p=.23, not significant.
limits: Tiny n, no control, skills test alpha .41, disposition scale alpha .53 at pretest. Text and tables contradict each other in places. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Doubt-type dispositions (skepticism) are the hardest to shift. That fits G1: do not rely on a trained urge to doubt; trigger doubt on signal.

source: Akcay, Karahan and Kara (2026) Critical thinking dispositions, problem solving and decision making (BMC Psychology 14:1277)
finding: In children, self-reported dispositions link to self-reported decision-making and success. Everything is self-report, so it measures confidence more than ability.
numbers: N=285 pupils aged 8-10. CTD->decision-making beta=.65; CTD->problem solving beta=.31; total effect on perceived success beta=.50; indirect via both mediators beta=.20, 95% CI [.095,.308].
quote: reliance on self-report scales, which may reflect confidence rather than actual ability
limits: Cross-sectional, self-report only, no performance test, text and table coefficients disagree.
agent_relevance: Shows the same-method inflation problem: disposition and outcome both self-rated give large paths. A model rating itself would behave the same.

source: Alpindo, Istiyono et al. (2024) Can critical-thinking skills be measured by analyzing metacognition? (J Teaching and Learning 18(2))
finding: Metacognition and critical thinking skill correlate strongly across studies, higher than dispositions correlate with skill in the longitudinal study above.
numbers: 60 effect sizes from 24 articles (Scopus 2013-2023): random-effects r=.649, 95% CI [.593,.704]. Strong at college, senior high, elementary; moderate at junior high and in non-Asian subgroup. Rosenthal fail-safe N 151125.
limits: English Scopus only; many custom scales; same-method self-report likely inflates r; one cited study found a negative correlation (Chang 2021). Heterogeneous.
agent_relevance: The habit that matters most may be monitoring (metacognition), which maps to a code-run check, not to a mood of open-mindedness.

source: Schoute and Alexander (2026) A critical analysis of critical thinking interventions in higher education (Review of Educational Research 96(4))
finding: 45 intervention studies (2010-2023): most defined critical thinking by observed practice, and measures often did not match the definition. Missing method detail weakens causal claims.
numbers: 45 studies. No pooled effect size reported on the page read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract page only; it does not split skills from dispositions.
agent_relevance: Reported intervention gains are weaker evidence than they look; do not import effect sizes into design decisions.

source: De Jesus (2024) Mind maps for critical-thinking skills and dispositions: a meta-analysis (Ed.D. dissertation, USF)
finding: Mind mapping raised critical thinking skill scores in quasi-experiments, with very high heterogeneity.
numbers: 22 studies, 1,535 participants. Skills g=0.73, 95% CI [0.65,0.81] (fixed effects), I2=97%. Collaborative maps g=1.53; 4-12 weeks g=1.54; digital g=0.72. Dispositions effect not on the page read.
limits: Abstract page; fixed-effects with I2=97% is questionable; all quasi-experimental; dissertation.
agent_relevance: Tool/scaffold support lifts skill scores; effect is on skill, dispositions not shown.

source: Effects of Generative AI Tools on Students' Critical Thinking: a three-level meta-analysis (Educational Psychology Review 2026)
finding: GenAI-supported learning is linked to higher critical thinking scores on average, but the effect is unstable.
numbers: 26 studies, 47 effect sizes, g=0.544, 95% CI [0.314,0.775], 95% prediction interval [-0.588,1.677] (includes zero), Q=280.99. Moderators: tutoring function and prescribed-use mode. Level, subject, duration, design not significant.
limits: Abstract page only; no skills vs dispositions split; includes low-quality designs.
agent_relevance: AI help can lift or lower thinking depending on how it is used; the prediction interval spanning zero is a warning.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Rationality Check! Benchmarking the rationality of large language models (arXiv 2509.14546)
finding: First benchmark to score LLMs on human thinking-disposition scales (Critical Thinking Disposition Scale, Actively Open-Minded Thinking, CRT, REI, Need for Cognition) next to reasoning tasks. Advanced models score at or above the human reference on dispositions.
numbers: Normalised-to-human scores (appendix table, 1.0 = human): Critical Thinking Disposition Scale 0.72, 0.86, 0.80, 0.80, 0.84, 0.93, 0.86 across seven models; AOT 0.72, 0.73, 0.71, 0.72, 0.71, 0.79, 0.71. Text: GPT-4o, GPT-4, DeepSeek v2.5, Qwen 7b/32b/72b, Bard beat humans on several reasoning tasks.
quote: in tasks like logical reasoning, including inductive, deductive, and causal reasoning, humans outperform LLMs
limits: Models answer a questionnaire about themselves; a stated disposition is not shown behaviour. Human reference taken from literature. Table columns not fully labelled in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Model self-report of open-mindedness is cheap and high. Do not read it as a guardrail. Behavioural tests (belief change on evidence) are the real measure.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Rationality Check!, gap between stated disposition and applied reasoning
finding: Advanced models look rational on scales and in theory but still fail on applied biases (illusion of control, bias blind spot, belief bias).
numbers: Humans beat LLMs on inductive, deductive and causal reasoning in the paper's text; models beat humans on regret aversion; DeepSeek and GPT-4o struggled with illusion of control, bias blind spot, belief bias.
limits: Single-run scoring; benchmark pools scales of different quality; models up to GPT-4o era.
agent_relevance: Disposition scores and task skill separate in LLMs too: skill versus disposition is a real gap here, not only in humans.

source: Triedman and Shmatikov (2025) MillStone: how open-minded are LLMs? (arXiv 2509.11967)
finding: Behavioural open-mindedness: with a neutral prompt, in-context human-written arguments shift model stances on contested issues. Authoritative sources sway models easily.
numbers: 107 issues, 517 pro arguments, 9 LLMs. 222 of 575 model-issue pairs (38.6%) have baseline stance at least 95% one side. Grok 3 open-mindedness score 39.2% above median. For four models some one-sided arguments shift stance the wrong way (Llama 3.1 8B: 12.2% shift toward a TikTok ban after anti-ban arguments).
quote: LLMs are open-minded on most issues. An authoritative source of information can easily sway an LLM's stance
limits: No normative claim about ideal level; contested non-factual issues, so no ground truth; GPT and Grok run only on the most controversial issues.
agent_relevance: Open-mindedness without a quality filter is gullibility. Pair any update with a check of the argument against output (G2, G5).

source: Triedman and Shmatikov (2025) MillStone, refusal and priors
finding: Claude models refuse stance questions on contested topics, but any supplied argument, even balanced, sharply lowers refusal. 21 issues showed unanimous strong priors across models.
numbers: Refusal rates for Opus 4: abortion 37.8%, sanctuary cities 68.9%, gun control 83.3%. 21 issues unanimous (all models at least 95% one side). Counter-argument shifts: Llama 8B 3 issues (6.1%), Opus 4 26 issues (3.0%).
limits: Opus 4 refusal behaviour is a model-specific policy.
agent_relevance: A disposition (refuse to take sides) is easily bypassed by context. Dispositions in prompts are weak controls.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: The habit of self-correction does not help without an outside signal. Intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after round 1 (41.8 after round 2); GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. 74.7% of GPT-3.5 GSM8K answers kept.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Test-set subsets (HotpotQA 100 items); prompt-sensitive; models from 2023.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and G2: willingness to self-correct is only a virtue when triggered by a real signal.

source: Huang et al. (2024) self-correction with oracle labels
finding: With ground-truth labels deciding when to correct, the same prompt gains a lot. The gain comes from the signal, not the model's judgement.
numbers: Oracle self-correct vs standard: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9->84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8->89.7, HotpotQA 26.0->29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5->97.5, CSQA 82.0->85.5, HotpotQA 49.0->59.0 (pairing of rows read from garbled extracted table, approximate).
limits: Oracle use is unrealistic; table layout garbled in extraction, so pairings are approximate.
agent_relevance: Revise only from real output; code supplies the stop/go signal.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (arXiv 2310.13548)
finding: The opposite failure: too-easy belief change. Challenged with 'Are you sure?', assistants drop correct answers and apologise.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions; accuracy falls by up to 27% (Claude 1.3) averaged over six datasets; models change initial answer between 32% (GPT-4) and 86% (Claude 1.3); user-suggested wrong answer cuts accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2).
quote: models tend to admit mistakes even when they didn't make a mistake
limits: Models of 2023; question sets are subsets; not all change is wrong.
agent_relevance: Open-mindedness must be tied to evidence quality, not to user pressure. A judge must not see the proposed answer (G5).

source: Sharma et al. (2023) sycophancy, preference data and models
finding: Human preference data and preference models reward agreement with the user, which trains the disposition in.
numbers: Logistic model of preference features holdout accuracy 71.3% (vs 72% for a 52B preference model). Matching user beliefs is among the most predictive features (up to 6% shift). For hard misconceptions the Claude 2 preference model prefers the sycophantic answer 45% of the time; best-of-4096 against it gives sycophantic output on about 75% vs about 25% with an oracle model.
limits: Single preference dataset (hh-rlhf helpfulness); effect per feature is small.
agent_relevance: Models carry a trained agreeableness bias; the schema must not rely on a model to resist it.

source: Pennycook, Cheyne, Barr, Koehler and Fugelsang (2015) On the reception and detection of pseudo-profound bullshit (Judgment and Decision Making 10(6))
finding: Analytic-thinking disposition and ability both predict lower acceptance of meaningless but profound-sounding text. Disposition and ability overlap.
numbers: Four studies, N=279, 187, 114, 232. BSR with CRT r=-.33 (S1); with heuristics-and-biases r=-.28 to -.36; with verbal intelligence r=-.37 (S1), -.30 (S2); with Raven r=-.26 (S2). Sensitivity with H&B r=.23 (S3).
limits: Correlational; MTurk and student samples; some scales low reliability (alpha .35-.67); 35.4% failed attention check in S1.
agent_relevance: Gullibility to fluent nonsense is the human analogue of an LLM accepting authoritative text.

source: Toward LLM-supported automated assessment of critical thinking subskills (arXiv 2510.12915; EDM 2026)
finding: GPT-5, Llama 3.1 8B and ModernBERT scored student essays on critical thinking subskills. Fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B did best where proficiency levels were clearly separable.
numbers: Three models; zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuned. Abstract page gave no kappa or dataset size.
limits: Abstract page only; assesses students, not the models' own thinking; skill side only.
agent_relevance: Skills of argumentation can be graded automatically; dispositions cannot be read from an essay.

source: Zaphir et al. (2024) How critically can an AI think? MAGE framework (arXiv 2406.14769)
finding: A framework for testing how well ChatGPT-4 can mimic critical thinking so teachers can judge assessment vulnerability.
numbers: Abstract page only: ChatGPT-4 tested; no numbers read.
limits: No measured results seen; educator-oriented.
agent_relevance: Low value for the schema; note only.

source: Wazan (2026) Strategies for creating uncertainty in the AI era to trigger students' critical thinking (arXiv 2602.00026)
finding: A proposal, not an experiment: use AI errors to trigger student reasoning. No LLM disposition test.
numbers: No experimental results. Rubric has 5 dimensions; evidence is one exam question and two example students.
quote: AI cannot be integrated into approaches that are already pedagogically weak.
limits: Rubric unvalidated; qualitative only.
agent_relevance: Consistent with doubt-on-signal: uncertainty is the trigger, not a standing mood.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis (Review of Educational Research)
finding: Teaching raises critical thinking outcomes modestly overall. Dialogue plus authentic problems plus mentoring worked best.
numbers: About 341 effect sizes, pooled g about 0.30 (recalled; not verified).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: Real training gains are small compared with the 3.0+ d values in single quasi-experiments.

source: Abrami et al. (2008) Instructional interventions affecting critical thinking skills and dispositions (Review of Educational Research)
finding: First big meta-analysis to separate skills and dispositions outcomes. Mixed (general plus immersion) approach with explicit instruction did best.
numbers: About 117 studies, 161 effect sizes, mean about 0.34 (recalled).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: Skills and dispositions are measured by different tests, so the split is real in the data.

source: Stanovich and West (1997, 2007, 2008) Actively open-minded thinking and myside bias
finding: Actively open-minded thinking predicts argument evaluation beyond cognitive ability; myside bias is largely independent of intelligence.
numbers: AOT-argument evaluation correlations around .3 to .4 after ability control; myside bias near zero correlation with ability (recalled).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: Dispositions add predictive value independent of capacity; both belong in the design. Ability alone does not remove bias.

source: Facione, Facione and Giancarlo (CCTDI, 1990s-2000) The disposition toward critical thinking
finding: The California CCTDI and the CCTST are weakly to moderately correlated, which supports treating skill and disposition as separable.
numbers: Reported correlations roughly r .1 to .4 across samples (recalled).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use. Some CCTDI subscales show weak reliability and factor structure in later work.
agent_relevance: Skill tests and attitude scales measure different things; do not infer one from the other.

source: Perkins, Jay and Tishman (1993) Beyond abilities: a dispositional theory of thinking (Merrill-Palmer Quarterly)
finding: Thinking failures come from three gaps: sensitivity to occasions, inclination, and ability. Many failures are not lack of ability.
numbers: Observation that students write one-sided arguments though able to write balanced ones (recalled; no figures).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: Sensitivity to occasions is the agent's S0/S6 detector: noticing when to doubt. Maps cleanly to G1.

source: Ennis (1996) Critical thinking dispositions: their nature and assessability (Informal Logic 18)
finding: Dispositions are hard to assess by self-report; Ennis argues for behavioural indicators and cautions against scale-based inference.
numbers: No pooled numbers (conceptual).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: Supports measuring agent dispositions by behaviour on probes, not by asking the agent.

source: Pennycook and Rand (2019) Lazy, not biased (Cognition 188)
finding: Susceptibility to fake news is better explained by lack of reflection than by motivated reasoning; cognitive reflection predicts better discernment regardless of political side.
numbers: Two studies, thousands of participants; CRT positively predicts discernment (recalled; no exact figures).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: Rival theory to bias accounts: laziness (a disposition to reflect) versus motive. Fits a trigger-based reflection design.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters (Perspectives on Psychological Science)
finding: Forecasting skill tracked intelligence, actively open-minded thinking and practice; training plus teaming also improved accuracy.
numbers: Training gain in Brier score about 10% in year 1 (recalled).
limits: Not opened this session; figures recalled from the literature and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: A field result where an open-minded disposition predicts calibrated performance even after ability controls.
